summary.text: Coastal upwelling is the best-known type of upwelling, where wind blowing along a coast brings deep water up to replace surface water near shore.
When the wind runs parallel to the coastline, Ekman transport carries surface water away from the coast, and deeper, colder, denser water rises in its place.
It supports some of the world's most productive fisheries, mainly along the Canary, Benguela, California and Humboldt currents.

facts.label: Strongest zone
facts.value: Off Luderitz, in the Benguela system

facts.label: Timing
facts.value: Year-round in some regions, seasonal in others

items.prompt: A steady wind blows parallel to a coastline. Which result would make deep water rise near the shore?

options.label: Surface water piles up against the coast
Surface water is carried away from the coast
Surface water flows straight along the shore
The sea near the coast stays perfectly still

items.explain: When Ekman transport moves surface water away from the coast, deeper, colder water rises to replace it.

items.prompt: Off the coast of Chile, in the Southern Hemisphere, which way are wind-driven currents turned?

options.label: To the right of the wind
Straight along with the wind
To the left of the wind
Straight back against the wind

items.explain: The Coriolis effect turns them to the left in the Southern Hemisphere and to the right in the Northern.

items.prompt: Roughly how fast does coastal upwelling normally lift water toward the surface?

options.label: About 5–10 meters per day
About 5–10 meters per second
About 5–10 kilometers per hour
About 5–10 centimeters per century

items.explain: Upwelling normally runs at about 5–10 meters per day, though wind strength can change that.

items.prompt: Fishing fleets off Peru, California and southern Africa share one natural advantage. What is it?

options.label: Warm water that draws in tropical fish
Calm seas with almost no wind
Shallow shelves covered in coral reef
Nutrient-rich deep water rising nearby

items.explain: These coasts lie on major upwelling currents, which bring nutrient-rich deep water up and support major fisheries.

items.prompt: Why is deep seawater rich in nutrients like nitrate and phosphate?

options.label: Dead plankton sink and decompose there
Undersea volcanoes keep releasing them
Rivers flow along the deep seafloor
Cold water turns sea salt into them

items.explain: The nutrients come from the decomposition of organic matter, such as dead plankton, sinking from the surface.

items.prompt: Once upwelled nutrients reach the sunlit surface, what puts them to use first?

options.label: Whales feeding close to the surface
Seabirds diving down for small fish
Phytoplankton, using photosynthesis
Worms living down on the seafloor

items.explain: Phytoplankton use the nutrients, carbon dioxide and sunlight to make organic compounds, and they sit at the base of the food chain.
